item.title: Long-term limits on maximum ice sheet thickness around central Antarctic Peninsula nunataks
item.dc:creator: Ryan North, Timothy T. Barrows, Klaus M. Wilcken, Finlay M. Stuart, Luigia Di Nicola, Anne Le Brocq, … (+1)
item.description:
Communications Earth & Environment — matched: ice sheet, Antarctic, Antarctica, deglaciation, last glacial maximum, cosmogenic, sea level, sea-level rise, numerical method
Understanding past ice sheet sensitivity to long-term climate cycles is essential to predict future sea-level rise. The Antarctic Peninsula Ice Sheet (APIS) is changing rapidly in one of Antarctica’s fastest warming regions. However, APIS thickness changes are poorly understood because there are limited terrestrial records of deglaciation. Here, the gap is filled by measuring cosmogenic nuclide ( 10 Be, 26 Al and 21 Ne) concentrations in 34 bedrock and boulder samples from high elevation nunataks in the APIS interior. Samples near the current ice surface record repeated burial by non-erosive ice mostly since ~890 ka. Nuclide ratios indicate that surfaces more than 121 – 170 m above current ice levels at Mount Faith, Mount Sullivan, and Engel Peaks have been ice-free for millions of years, reaching production-decay-erosion equilibrium with erosion rates as low as 0.14 ± 0.02 m Myr -1 . These limits contrast with numerical models which predict >250 m of thinning since the last glacial maximum, suggesting they are overestimating sea-level contribution from the central and eastern Antarctic Peninsula.

item.title: Basal sliding and ice rheology in West Antarctica constrained by multi-epoch satellite observations
item.dc:creator: Jan De Rydt
item.description:
Journal of Glaciology — matched: ice sheet, ice stream, ice rheology, glacier, Antarctica, sea level, sea-level rise, Bayesian
A new method for the calibration of uncertain parameters in large-scale viscous ice-flow models is presented, with particular focus on the basal sliding law and ice rheology.The approach combines Bayesian inference with the rich information contained in successive satellite observations of ice-sheet elevation and velocity changes, and does not require knowledge of the surface or basal mass balance.The method is validated on a synthetic glacier with known physics, and subsequently applied to West Antarctica.The results support earlier evidence for a plastic basal rheology and strongly non-Newtonian creep within the regions ice streams.The stochastic framework provides a robust foundation for improved predictive simulations, offering data-driven constraints on how basal sliding and ice rheology may influence West Antarcticas future contribution to sea-level rise.

item.title: Greenland ice sheet retreat intensifies the African monsoon through a polar-tropical atmospheric teleconnection
item.dc:creator: Zixuan Han, Ran Feng, Zhenqian Wang, Xiangyu Li, Zhongshi Zhang, Tianchen He, … (+4)
item.description:
Nature Communications — matched: ice sheet, Greenland, polar, Arctic, paleoclimate, Pliocene, proxy, global warming
Global climate forcing drives major changes in the North African summer monsoon (NASM), yet how high-latitude cryospheric changes influence tropical hydroclimate through atmospheric dynamics remains unclear. Integrating paleoclimate proxy evidence with coupled climate-model simulations, sensitivity experiments, and idealized atmospheric modeling, we show that Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) retreat acts as a dynamically important amplifier of NASM rainfall. Using the mid-Pliocene as a natural experiment for sustained global warming, we find that NASM rainfall was markedly stronger than that simulated under transient future warming for comparable global-mean temperature increases. GrIS retreat enhances Arctic warming, thereby perturbing the upper-tropospheric westerly jet and triggering a stationary Rossby wave train linking Greenland to North Africa. This polar–tropical atmospheric teleconnection strengthens monsoon circulation and moisture convergence, producing wetter conditions across the Sahara–Sahel. These results reveal a high-latitude pathway through which slow cryospheric changes modulate low-latitude monsoon variability under sustained warming.

item.title: Mountain carbon budgets miss cryosphere hazard events
item.dc:creator: Chunlin Song, Qiongwei Gu, Biqiong Wu, Genxu Wang
item.description:
Frontiers in Environmental Science — matched: cryosphere, glacier, Arctic, sediment core, radiocarbon, permafrost, climate feedback, CO2
Warming is destabilizing the mountain cryosphere and triggering more frequent hazard events. These hazards mobilize large stores of carbon as well as rock, ice and water. Yet mountain carbon budgets largely overlook this flux, because routine monitoring rarely operates at the time, location and resolution that hazard events demand. We argue that cryosphere hazards should be treated as carbon events and set out how to close the gap. Here, cryosphere hazard events are mass movements in glacial and permafrost terrain whose onset is abrupt relative to gradual degradation, together with the cascades they trigger (Ding et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2025). They range from rock-ice avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) lasting hours to retrogressive thaw slumps that develop within days to years as a form of abrupt thaw (Turetsky et al., 2020).At high elevations, warming is often amplified (Pepin et al., 2015(Pepin et al., , 2025)). Global glacier mass-loss rates rose by 36 ± 10% between 2000-2011and 2012-2023(Zemp et al., 2025)), and mountain permafrost is warming (Wu and Zhang, 2008;Noetzli et al., 2024) and thawing abruptly (Turetsky et al., 2020). GLOF frequency in the Third Pole has risen since 1980 (Zhang et al., 2023), and global GLOFs from moraine-dammed lakes increased from 5.2 to 15.2 per year between 1981-1990and 2011-2020(Zhang et al., 2025)). Retrogressive thaw slumps are spreading rapidly in alpine permafrost (Xia et al., 2024), driving cascading damage locally and downstream (Ding et al., 2021;Shugar et al., 2021). Existing frameworks recognize erosion, lateral transport, and outgassing as carbon pathways (Chapin et al., 2006;Hilton and West, 2020;Regnier et al., 2022), but lack a way to quantify hazard-driven mobilization and trace its fate (Figure 1a).A complete net ecosystem carbon budget needs vertical exchange from eddy covariance and chambers, and lateral export and outgassing from river and lake sampling (Chapin et al., 2006;Keenan and Williams, 2018), yet these observations rarely capture brief events or hillslope-channel transport.Three monitoring problems limit how cryosphere hazards enter carbon budgets. Temporal aliasing means periodic monitoring misses an event when the sampling interval exceeds a hazard-driven concentration peak. Extrapolation error means that, once a hazard resets sediment and carbon availability, pre-event concentration-discharge relationships no longer predict post-event fluxes. Material selectivity means that sampling of dissolved and suspended loads excludes carbon moved as woody debris, coarse bedload, or buried in deposits. No single method can constrain these fluxes: atmospheric observations cannot resolve lateral transfers, and satellite erosion detection cannot quantify the concentration or reactivity of displaced material. Figure 1. (a) Conceptual diagram showing cryosphere hazards-induced mobilization, transport, and transformation of carbon along a hazard-to-fate cascade. Cryosphere hazards, including glacier detachment, rock-ice avalanche, glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) and thaw slump, connect mountain carbon stores to downstream environments. Cascading flows entrain carbon from soils, rock debris and vegetation, transporting it through channels to valley floors and receiving waters. Along these pathways, decomposition can release carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4), whereas deposition and burial can retain carbon and vegetation recovery can restore CO2 uptake. Subsequent remobilization can expose stored material to further transport and decomposition, extending carbon effects beyond the initial disturbance. Whether a disturbance increases or decreases net carbon transfer to the atmosphere depends on carbon fate and ecosystem uptake, evaluated against a no-event trajectory over the same area and period. The diagram presents a conceptual accounting framework, not a quantified carbon budget, and unquantified pathways should not be read as zero fluxes. Over an accounting period, stock change within the boundary is ΔCstock = -Fatm -Fexport (Eq. 1), where Fatm is the cumulative net carbon flux to the atmosphere and Fexport is the net lateral export across the boundary, both positive when carbon leaves the system; burial within the boundary redistributes carbon within ΔCstock. The event term is □□!"!#$ = ∑ [□□ %$&,!"!#$($) -□□ %$&,*!+($) ] $ ! $ "(Eq. 2), relative to a no-event trajectory; Eevent > 0 indicates a source. POC, particulate organic carbon; DOC, dissolved organic carbon; DIC, dissolved inorganic carbon. (b) Gaps in representing cryosphere hazard events in mountain carbon budgets and ways forward.The consequence is systematic omission rather than random error. Hazard-driven fluxes are rare, brief and often occur in inaccessible terrain, so the disturbance-transfer term in the net ecosystem carbon balance usually lacks an empirical estimate and is underestimated. Known hazard fluxes come almost entirely from bespoke post-event surveys; after a GLOF, channelarmour disruption exposed sediment invisible to pre-event rating curves (Cook et al., 2018).The magnitude missed varies, so no single correction factor works across events. Earthquakeand storm-triggered landslides, used here as process analogues because their carbon export has been measured, show this variability. Landslide pulses increased biospheric carbon export (Hilton et al., 2008;Wang et al., 2016) and accounted for roughly 40% of organic carbon export in two New Zealand catchments (Howarth et al., 2025), whereas the Gorkha earthquake produced no detectable perturbation (Märki et al., 2021). Atmospheric inversions constrain aggregate CO2 exchange without attributing sources (Ciais et al., 2022), so a hazard signal may already sit within them unresolved.Cryosphere hazard cascades mobilize carbon spanning orders of magnitude in age and lability, from millennial permafrost organic matter and petrogenic rock carbon to recently fixed vegetation (Figure 1a). Source areas above treeline hold little biomass, but downstream cascades cross carbon-rich soils and forests. The 2023 South Lhonak disaster released about 50 million m 3 of water and eroded about 270 million m 3 of sediment (Sattar et al., 2025), yet its carbon was not estimated. A simple calculation shows the scale at stake. Assume a dry bulk density of 1.3-1.8 t/m 3 (Ji et al., 2020) and an organic carbon content of 0.43-0.79% for landslide debris from the Tibetan Plateau (Wang et al., 2023). The ~91 million m 3 of debris (excluding ice) detached at the China-Nepal border in 2026 (Li et al., 2026) would then hold roughly 0.51-1.29 Tg of organic carbon. That gross lateral mobilization is about 2.5-6.5 times the annual biospheric organic carbon export of the much larger Narayani catchment (Märki et al., 2021, their Fig. 4), mobilized in a few hours. This ratio is an upper bound, because the debris carbon also includes petrogenic carbon. Whether this carbon is flushed downstream, buried, or oxidized in the valley, it falls outside budgets built on routine river sampling.Mobilization changes the conditions that regulate decomposition. Aggregate disruption and exposure can increase microbial access, whereas mineral association and rapid burial may protect organic matter (Hilton and West, 2020). Carbon age alone does not determine lability.Old yet bioavailable dissolved organic matter occurs in Alaskan glacial runoff (Hood et al., 2009), and old carbon contributes substantially to river CO2 emissions (Dean et al., 2025). At permafrost thaw slumps, vegetation-free surfaces reduced respiration by about one-half but gross primary productivity by about four-fifths (Jiang et al., 2026a), and a plateau-wide synthesis found lower respiration in collapsed areas but increased CH4 release in alpine swamp meadows (Jia et al., 2026). Floods bury soil and biomass in valley fills, lakes and reservoirs, while channel reworking can later expose them. Drained thermokarst and proglacial lake beds and debris-flow surfaces are a particular blind spot, because dry inland waters can still emit carbon (Keller et al., 2020). The fate of mobilized carbon depends jointly on transport speed and reaction kinetics. Rapid flushing through cold, sediment-rich channels can export carbon before substantial mineralization, whereas retention in oxygenated sediments prolongs microbial breakdown.Hazards also mobilize inorganic carbon, exposing reactive minerals and changing waterrock interactions (Hawkings et al., 2026). Carbonic acid weathering and carbonation can consume CO2 (Styllas et al., 2026), whereas sulfide oxidation coupled to carbonate dissolution can release it (Hilton and West, 2020), and oxidation of petrogenic organic carbon is another CO2 source (Zondervan et al., 2023). In Tibetan Plateau rivers, net weathering is estimated to offset about 35% of river CO2 emissions (Zhang et al., 2026). Because hazard events mix inorganic and organic carbon, assessments based only on organic carbon decomposition may miss part of the response (Middelburg, 2024). The same mobilization couples carbon with other element cycles: permafrost thaw can increase N2O emissions (Voigt et al., 2020), glacial erosion exports reactive phosphorus (Hawkings et al., 2016), and thaw slumps release permafrost mercury, sharply raising methylmercury concentrations downstream (Schuster et al., 2018;St. Pierre et al., 2018).Whether a hazard event is a carbon source or sink depends on the quantity, boundary and processes assessed. Gross mobilization is the displacement of carbon from its original location, outlet export its transfer across a defined boundary, and net atmospheric exchange its transfer to or from the atmosphere. Redeposition within the same boundary redistributes carbon without creating a landscape sink, so these quantities should be accounted for separately and reconciled through mass balance (Eq. 1, Figure 1). We define the event term (Eq. 2, Figure 1) as cumulative net atmospheric carbon exchange with the event minus that under a specified no-event trajectory. Positive values indicate additional release or reduced uptake (a source), and negative values indicate additional uptake or avoided release (a sink). The reference site should share the affected site's warming and hydrology, differing only in the absence of the hazard. An event can thus increase atmospheric carbon relative to this reference while the landscape remains a net sink. Burial and ecological recovery can offset part of the disturbance, although forested-landslide evidence should be applied cautiously to alpine terrain. Post-Wenchuan sediment storage and revegetation raised carbon mass by about 10% (Liu et al., 2026), whereas greenness recovery after tundra thaw slumps took a decade at low-Arctic sites and more than 30 years at high-Arctic and highelevation sites (Xia et al., 2026). Greenness recovery does not imply recovered soil carbon stocks or net ecosystem exchange, so persistent productivity losses may matter even when deposited organic matter decomposes slowly.The atmospheric benefit of burial also depends on the reference trajectory. Relocating organic matter that would otherwise have remained protected adds little, whereas preserving material that would otherwise decompose avoids emissions (Galy et al., 2007). Only regrowth exceeding the no-event trajectory lowers the event term, and preserving petrogenic organic carbon averts a geological release without removing fixed atmospheric carbon. These distinctions keep sediment accumulation from supporting unwarranted sequestration claims.Field observations constrain exchange at some thaw slumps, geomorphic reconstructions constrain mobilization pathways, and downstream studies constrain delayed transport, yet few link all three within one event. Assessments should also report CO2-C and CH4-C separately, and converting CH4 emissions into a forcing metric requires an explicit metric and time horizon.We propose four priorities to close this gap (Figure 1b). First, establish a common accounting basis. Each assessment should specify its spatial boundary, accounting period, carbon forms and disturbance coverage, carry unsampled intervals into the uncertainty (Chapin et al., 2006;Ciais et al., 2022), and report mobilization, boundary export and the event term separately (Figure 1, Eqs. 1-2). This separates fluxes missing from an assessment from disturbance effects included but not attributed. Shared event identifiers should connect hazard inventories, water samples, deposit surveys and gas-flux records, distinguishing new erosion from remobilization of previously surveyed material (Jiang et al., 2026b).Second, trace carbon from source areas through transport pathways to deposits. Converting eroded volumes into carbon mass requires source material measurements that capture differences among lithologies, soil horizons, particle sizes and woody debris, with uncertainty in ice content and dry density propagated. Provenance measurements should distinguish biospheric from petrogenic carbon, because depleted radiocarbon alone cannot separate the two, and water chemistry should constrain weathering pathways and their CO2 uptake or release (Hilton and West, 2020). Post-event deposits record retained material but cannot reconstruct the dissolved and fine particulate carbon exported during the event (Märki et al., 2021).Third, connect short-lived transport pulses to longer-term carbon effects. Pre-positioned automatic samplers and redundant stream sensors can capture flood dynamics where deployment is safe (Cook et al., 2018). Later observations should track channel deposits, exposed lake beds, soil gas exchange and vegetation through successive seasons (Keller et al., 2020;Xia et al., 2026). Paired disturbed and reference sites separate event effects from regional change, and sediment cores can extend instrumental records if chronology and postdepositional carbon loss are treated explicitly (Howarth et al., 2025).Fourth, represent event diversity and overlapping legacies in regional models. Multiplying event frequency by a single mean carbon yield obscures differences among carbon-poor headwaters, vegetated valleys and efficient depositional traps. Models should link mobilization to carbon provenance, connectivity, transformation and ecological recovery, while allowing event recurrence to change and later floods to remobilize earlier deposits. Comparison with independent outlet fluxes or stock changes over a common period can show whether explicit event representation improves budget estimates.The approach generates testable expectations. Events crossing carbon-rich terrain with direct channel connections should mobilize more biospheric carbon than events confined to mineral debris (Hilton and West, 2020). Stable deposits should retain carbon longer than frequently reworked channels, and slow revegetation should prolong reductions in uptake.Testing these expectations would show where event accounting changes the inferred mountain carbon balance. Cryosphere hazards are becoming more frequent as warming continues (Ding et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2025;Jiang et al., 2026b;Richter, 2026), so the carbon they mobilize is a growing budget term, and closing the observational gap is necessary to determine its climate feedback.

item.title: Evaluation of reanalysis datasets for studying high-elevation meteorological conditions in the Langtang Catchment, Nepal
item.dc:creator: Gunjan Silwal, Bethan J. Davies, Rachel Joanne Carr, Owen King, Sammie Buzzard
item.description:
Frontiers in Earth Science — matched: glacier, surface melt, surface energy balance, albedo, reanalysis, downscaling
Climate reanalysis datasets are widely used in hydro-meteorological and cryospheric research across High Mountain Asia (HMA), where in situ observations are scarce. Here, we evaluate ERA5L, High Asian Refined Analysis (HARv2), Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications (MERRA2), and Climatologies at High Resolution for the Earth’s Land Surface Areas (CHELSA) against near-surface meteorological observations between 3,865 and 5,350 m a.s.l., in the upper Langtang Catchment, Nepal, using statistical metrics and Taylor Skill Score ( TSS ). We further assess their suitability for glacier surface energy balance (SEB) and mass balance modelling. No reanalysis product consistently outperforms the others; rather, their performance varies by meteorological variable, site, surface conditions, and timescale, with generally better performance at glacier sites, likely because their relatively homogeneous surface conditions are more readily represented by reanalysis products. Near-surface air temperature ( T 2m ) and humidity (specific: q and relative: RH ) are well reproduced ( TSS > 0.77) across products, although cold temperature and both dry and moist humidity biases are pervasive across sites. Wind speed ( u ) is poorly represented across products, sites, and timescales, reflecting their limited ability to resolve boundary layer processes and local katabatic and anabatic flows. Precipitation also exhibits large discrepancies, with ERA5L and HARv2 overestimating precipitation totals by ∼89–232% and MERRA2 and CHELSA underestimating by 30%–60%. They also generate frequent wet days and early-afternoon convective rainfall, in contrast to observed late-afternoon and nocturnal-to-early morning maxima. Hourly and daily SEB simulations at the Yala-on-Glacier site driven by reanalysis forcings yield statistically significant surface melt relative to reference estimates driven by in situ datasets; however, substantial differences in magnitude exist among products. ERA5L and HARv2 exhibit relatively small errors, largely due to compensating errors between radiative and turbulent fluxes, whereas MERRA2 and CHELSA show larger melt discrepancies due to their large radiative flux errors and underestimated precipitation that affects the surface albedo. Overall, our results underscore both the usefulness and limitations of reanalysis products for cryospheric applications in complex mountainous catchments and emphasize the need for assimilation of high-elevation observations in reanalysis products, alongside improved downscaling approaches, to better resolve local-scale atmospheric processes.

item.title: A valley system investigation of Holocene coastal change and Irish Sea palaeogeography in Cardigan Bay, Wales, UK
item.dc:creator: Caitlin Nagle, Robert Johnston, Katherine Selby
item.description:
Boreas — matched: Holocene, proxy, sea level, sea-level rise, relative sea level
Of the three substantial areas of postglacial aerial exposure on the Irish Sea shelf (Liverpool Bay, Cardigan Bay and the Bristol Channel), Cardigan Bay is the largest and the one about which we know the least. This article provides the first empirical sea level data for Cardigan Bay since the 1980s. It examines the proposition that the valleys of north Cardigan Bay were subject to a long period of marine influence that is not modelled in current palaeogeographical reconstructions. Detailed lithostratigraphic investigations traced the extent of Early to Mid‐Holocene marine influence in the Dysynni valley. Multiple microfossil proxies were used to calculate sea level data points. Two sea level index points from a back‐barrier marsh indicated relative sea level rise from −5.55 to −3.13 mOD between 7790–7630 and 6399–6296 cal. a BP. Freshwater/terrestrial limiting points from 7 km inland bracketed a period of marine influence between 9889–9545 and 4783–4416 cal. a BP. Pollen recorded a transition from saltmarsh, fen and reed‐swamp environments to alder carr and then birch woodland. The results were combined with existing lithostratigraphic and biostratigraphic data to show that the overdeepened glacial valleys of north Cardigan Bay were subject to marine influence from before 12 000 cal. a BP, with different palaeogeographical histories dependent on their depths and rates of postglacial sedimentation.

item.title: Spatial Shift in Southern Ocean Seasonal Ice Zone Production Trends
item.dc:creator: Chao Zhang, Anmin Duan, Bingxian Liu
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: meltwater, albedo, tipping point, Southern Ocean
In recent decades, satellite observations have reported a marked increase in primary production across the Seasonal Ice Zone (SIZ) of the Southern Ocean, indicating enhanced ecosystem activity and a potential rise in biological carbon storage. However, the spatial coherence and temporal stability of these trends remain poorly constrained. Here, using satellite observations and model-based data from 1998/99 to 2023/24, we detect two successive regime shifts in austral summer SIZ primary production. The first, around 2007/08, marks a transition from a dipole—characterized by declining production in the Weddell Sea and increasing production in the Amundsen Sea—to a basin-wide increase across the SIZ. The second, around 2014/15, represents an intensification of this basin-wide pattern under accelerated sea-ice loss. Mechanistically, the initial 2007/08 structural shift is likely triggered by the reversal of the Southern Annular Mode (SAM), which restructured regional sea-ice distribution via rapid Ekman-driven atmospheric forcing. For the post-2007/08 period, sea-ice redistribution fundamentally altered light penetration, while wind-driven mixed-layer shoaling further enhanced light availability, promoting a widespread rebound in primary production. In contrast, the slow response to persistent SAM forcing—via enhanced Circumpolar Deep Water upwelling—progressively decreased sea-ice concentration, reaching a critical tipping point around 2014/15 that accelerated the basin-wide sea-ice decline. For the post-2014/15 period, the accelerated sea-ice loss directly reduced surface albedo and introduced substantial meltwater, which further shoaled the mixed layer, collectively driving a stronger productivity increase. These results have implications for projecting future changes in regional primary production and assessing the broader impacts on the Southern Ocean's biological carbon pump.

item.title: Bioclimatic and habitat signals in Pleistocene fluvial microvertebrate assemblages from the Middle Dnipro region, Ukraine
item.dc:creator: Lilia Popova, Alina Mishta, Vadym Yanenko, Tetiana Myronchuk, Oleksandr Kovalchuk
item.description:
Journal of Quaternary Science — matched: Arctic, paleoclimate, interglacial, MIS stage, Quaternary
Fluvial microvertebrate assemblages are important but underexplored archives for reconstructing Quaternary environments, particularly in regions lacking karstic and cave deposits. We analyse late Middle and early Late Pleistocene small‐vertebrate assemblages from the Middle Dnipro region, Ukraine, to compare two interpretative frameworks: habitat‐weighting analysis and bioclimatic spectra. The studied assemblages span multiple Marine Isotope Stages (MIS 11 to MIS 5) and derive exclusively from alluvial contexts characterised by taphonomic overprinting and time‐averaging. Using principal component analysis, we compare the environmental signals extracted by both methods across different taxonomic datasets. In both approaches, the dominant source of variation reflects changes in ecological evenness, expressed as shifts in the relative importance of steppe, tundra–steppe and high‐latitude taxa. The most even assemblages correspond to cold‐stage conditions and are characterised by arctic and boreal elements, whereas low‐evenness assemblages are dominated by core tundra–steppe taxa. Habitat spectra additionally capture geomorphological influences related to river‐valley dynamics, resulting in a diffuse climatic signal. In contrast, bioclimatic spectra more directly resolve glacial–interglacial climatic gradients and show greater robustness to incomplete faunal lists and taphonomic biases. Our results demonstrate that bioclimatic spectra provide a clearer palaeoclimatic signal than habitat‐based approaches for fluvial microvertebrate assemblages. This method is therefore particularly well suited to Quaternary environmental reconstruction in lowland river systems affected by taphonomic and sedimentary filtering.

item.title: A small ensemble of bias-adjusted CMIP6 climate simulations over North America extending to 2300
item.dc:creator: Émilie Bresson, Juliette Lavoie, Asli Bese, Anne-Sophie Fortin, David Huard, Travis Logan, … (+1)
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: Earth system model, Earth system, CMIP, ensemble
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Even if many sectors would benefit from scientific evidence on the long-term consequences of current policy choices, most climate projections end in 2100. This paper describes a collection of bias-adjusted climate simulations extending to 2300. It includes few Earth System Models, most of them driven by scenarios at the very low or very high end of the range of plausible futures. The composition of the ensemble makes it difficult to deliver climate services supporting climate risk assessments.

item.title: Attribution of climate extremes with global temperature regressions: accounting for uncertainty from internal variability
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Kotz, Markus G. Donat
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: ensemble, climate extreme, climate change
Attribution of climate change to anthropogenic forcing is an important goal in climate science. Regression of local conditions on global temperatures is a popular statistical approach, but whether the uncertainty derived from observations alone can reflect the range of outcomes possible due to internal variability remains unclear. Here, we use large ensembles from three climate models as an idealized testbed to quantify the role of internal variability for such attribution of climate extremes with single climate realisations. Internal variability generates large uncertainty in the linear-regression slope between global temperatures and regional temperature extremes, exceeding 40% of the ensemble mean slope across 50, 38, and 9% of the global surface area in the MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-LR and CanESM5 models respectively. Nevertheless, we show that these uncertainties can be accurately inferred from individual ensemble members using a block-bootstrap procedure - offering potential for a robust application to observations. Block-bootstrapping also accurately captures the absolute uncertainty for precipitation extremes, despite a substantially smaller signal-to-noise ratio which leads to underestimated and overly noisy estimates of relative uncertainty at present-day warming levels. This work provides a basis for the attribution of climate extremes from observations which can robustly capture the uncertainty associated with internal climate variability.

item.title: Quantifying the role of temporal-scale-dependent precipitation change in mass balance in the Dongkemadi Glacier, Tibetan Plateau
item.dc:creator: Liqiao Liang, Lan Cuo, Qiang Liu, Xiaobo He
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: glacier, meltwater, albedo
Understanding how precipitation changes affect glaciers is critical for predicting their future responses as well as for forecasting water supplies and potential impacts on downstream lowland regions. This study evaluated the effects of precipitation changes at annual, seasonal, and monthly scales on the mass balance of the Dongkemadi (DKMD) Glacier (central Tibetan Plateau) during 1960–2009. Results showed increasing trends in precipitation at the annual, seasonal, and monthly scales, except in July (decreasing trend). Warm season (i.e., the glacier’s melt season) precipitation constituted 91.4% of annual precipitation, and accounted for 80.3% of the annual precipitation increase. A comparison of precipitation changes effects across the three scales revealed: i) All three precipitation trends increased annual, warm season and monthly glacier mass balance, except in July; ii) Using monthly precipitation trends captured the monthly variability of precipitation-induced mass balance changes (range: 50 mm w.e.); iii) Annual or seasonal precipitation trends underestimated mass balance changes by approximately 22%; iv) The direct driver of mass balance increase was enhanced mass inputs (i.e., snowfall) from increased precipitation, which accounted for over half of the total increase in mass balance; and v) The indirect driver was reduced melt energy, primarily attributed to decreased net shortwave radiation caused by higher surface albedo. This study confirms the effectiveness of using monthly precipitation trends to investigate how precipitation changes impacted on the DKMD Glacier and its meltwater runoff. Furthermore, it provides valuable insights for accurately assessing precipitation changes effects on the energy and mass balance of glaciers globally.

item.dc:creator: Jung-A Yang
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: sea level
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Extreme sea levels on the Korean coast come mostly with typhoons. Kor_SeaLevel was built from 70 years of hourly records at 49 tide gauges: each record is split into tide, mean sea level and storm surge, checked for errors and linked to the 270 typhoons that affected Korea. The database agrees with official tide products to within centimeters and shows where global storm surge models depart from local observations.

item.title: Retreating glaciers and snow cover are amplifying summer droughts in the upper Adige River Basin (Italy)
item.dc:creator: Susen Shrestha, Stefano Terzi, Davide Zoccatelli, Mattia Zaramella, Marco Borga, Andrea Galletti, … (+4)
item.category: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
item.description:
Natural hazards and earth system sciences — matched: glacier, meltwater, climate change
Snow and glacier meltwater play a critical role in sustaining summer streamflow in mountains and downstream regions. Yet, understanding glaciers' contributions to buffer river streamflow during droughts remains limited and poses major barriers to improve present and future water management within the context of climate change. This study evaluates the contribution of glacier melt to summer flows and its role in mitigating hydrological droughts in the upper Adige River basin (Italy). We developed and implemented a new dynamic glacier module into the ICHYMOD-TOPMELT hydrological model, annually updating glacier area and improving the quantification of meltwater contributions under progressive glacier retreat (from 111 km 2 in 1997 to 79 km 2 in 2017). The hydrological model exhibited robust performance (KGE = 0.89 for 1997–2022 for the whole upper Adige River basin at the Bronzolo closing station; 0.88 in summers) capturing observed glacier area, mass balance, and seasonal melt trends. Results show that glacier melt in the upper Adige River basin contributed an average of 4.5 % to total summer streamflow during 1997–2022, with significant spatial variability, reaching 30 % in glacierized subbasins. During the severe droughts of 2003, 2005 and 2022, glacier melt contributions ranged between 4 % and 12 % at the upper Adige closing section. In 2003, high temperature and limited Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) led to glacier melt accounting for 11.67 % of summer flows. By contrast, the significant runoff deficit in 2005 was driven by colder temperatures, which reduced glacier melt contributions to 4.85 %, combined with low SWE conditions. In 2022, the combination of low precipitation, low snow cover and high temperature drove glacier melt. In contrast to the 2003 drought, reduced glacier areas led to lower absolute contributions (8.17 %). Our findings reveal that despite the increased melt rates in recent warm years, retreating glacier areas have reduced their absolute buffering effect. Glacier retreat is weakening the contribution of glaciers to summer flows, increasing the upper Adige River basin's dependence on precipitation and snowmelt, the latter of which is also showing a decreasing trend. For these reasons, accounting for dynamic glacier and snow changes is essential to improve future drought projections and inform adaptive water management in glacier-fed basins within the context of climate and anthropogenic changes.

item.title: North Atlantic Modulation of the 1931 Extreme East Asian Summer Flood Revealed by Large-Ensemble Seasonal Forecasts
item.dc:creator: Yueqi Zhou, Shuai Hu, Wanheng Ye, Tianjun Zhou, Bo Wu, Lixia Zhang, … (+1)
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: predictability, reanalysis, ensemble
Extreme precipitation during May-July 1931 caused severe flooding over East Asia, with devastating societal impacts. The mechanisms and predictability of this event remain uncertain because sparse early-twentieth-century observations limit robust attribution based on a single reanalysis realization. Here, we use a century-long 51-member CSF-20C seasonal hindcast to examine the predictability and dynamical drivers of the 1931 flood from an ensemble perspective. In this framework, the ensemble mean represents the predictable signal, whereas the inter-member spread represents the unpredictable component that is not constrained by the common initial conditions. The ensemble mean reproduces the tropical Indo-Pacific SST anomalies and the western North Pacific anomalous anticyclone, but the predicted rainband is displaced southward relative to observations, indicating that the predictable signal alone is insufficient to determine the observed rainband location. Individual members that better reproduce the observed rainfall pattern reveal a key role for extratropical modulation. The leading inter-member EOF mode explains 50.06% of the precipitation spread over eastern China and is associated with a Eurasian mid- to high-latitude wave train linked to a North Atlantic tripole-like SST pattern. This wave train modulates the East Asian upper-level jet, enhances ascent over eastern China, and shifts the rainband northward toward its observed location. Surface turbulent heat-flux anomalies and idealized linear baroclinic model experiments further support the physical plausibility of a North Atlantic influence. These results indicate that the 1931 flood arose from a predictable signal whose regional expression was modulated by North Atlantic-related extratropical circulation variability. Our study based on large-sample seasonal hindcasts offers a transferable framework for attributing extreme climate events.

item.title: Urban climate dynamics in informal settlements: Spatiotemporal rainfall and temperature variability in Thembelihle, Johannesburg
item.dc:creator: Sailas Hussein Matamanda, Walter Musakwa, Armstrong Dzomba
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: climate dynamics, climate change
by Sailas Hussein Matamanda, Walter Musakwa, Armstrong Dzomba Climate change has emerged as a critical contemporary concern, marked by greater variability and severity in weather systems, from extreme heat to drought and intense precipitation. Africa is particularly vulnerable, with urban settlements facing disproportionate risks. This study investigates long-term temperature and rainfall dynamics in Thembelihle, an informal settlement in Johannesburg, alongside broader metropolitan trends, using robust statistical and geospatial methods. Temperature and rainfall data spanning five decades (1974–2024 for Thembelihle; 1981–2024 for Johannesburg) were examined using the non-parametric Mann-Kendall (MK) Test and Sen’s Slope estimation to detect monotonic trends. Rainfall indices included the number of wet days (NWDT), the highest number of consecutive wet days (HNCWD), the highest number of consecutive dry days (HNCDD), and the maximum daily rainfall (HRPD). Extreme temperature events in Thembelihle were examined using a Peak Over Threshold (POT) approach. Spatial interpolation of CHIRPS rainfall and ERA5 temperature anomalies was conducted in QGIS to visualize spatiotemporal variability across Johannesburg. Results reveal statistically significant warming in Thembelihle, with minimum temperatures increasing at 0.0505 °C/year and maximum temperatures at 0.0391 °C/year, remaining higher than Johannesburg’s anomaly trend, although the magnitude of this difference is reduced when trends are compared over a harmonised temporal baseline (1981–2024). Extreme heat events, though historically rare, have clustered in recent years, signalling emerging instability. Rainfall patterns in Thembelihle show high interannual variability with no significant long-term decline, though spring rainfall exhibits a borderline decreasing trend. Johannesburg’s rainfall metrics highlight intensifying extremes: longer dry spells (+1 day/year) and higher maximum daily rainfall (+0.30 mm/year). Drought analysis identifies overlapping severe years (1984, 1999, 2003), underscoring regional susceptibility, while Thembelihle’s higher variability points to localized vulnerability. Spatial analysis confirms rainfall gradients, with wetter conditions in the northeast and drier conditions in the south, alongside localized temperature hotspots. These findings demonstrate a dual climate challenge: accelerating heat stress and increasingly variable rainfall. Informal settlements such as Thembelihle are disproportionately exposed, requiring both water resource coordination and localized adaptation strategies.

item.title: Hydroclimatic evolution under changing westerly–monsoon influences in northeastern China since the Late Glacial
item.dc:creator: Yi Huang, Hongwei Meng, 建波 朱, Dongbo Wang, Zeyang Zhu, Jing Wu
item.description:
PLoS ONE — matched: paleoclimate, Holocene
Hydroclimatic variability in the transition zone between the East Asian summer monsoon and mid-latitude westerlies reflects the combined influence of these two circulation systems. Understanding how their relative influences have changed over time is essential for interpreting long-term regional moisture variability. Here, we reconstructed regional hydroclimatic changes since 14.3 ka BP using a continuous lacustrine sequence from Aranji Nur, a closed lake on the southwestern margin of the Hulunbuir Grassland in northeastern China. Sediment grain-size distributions were analyzed and compared with regional paleoclimate and environmental records. Four major hydroclimatic stages were identified: relatively dry conditions during 14.3-9.2 ka BP, increased effective moisture during 9.2-4.8 ka BP, gradually declining moisture during 4.8-1.5 ka BP, and renewed aridification since 1.5 ka BP. Variations in sediment grain size, particularly sand content, were broadly consistent with changes in regional moisture availability and surface stability, reflecting the combined effects of vegetation cover, sediment availability, aeolian transport, and local depositional processes. Comparison with regional records suggests that increased moisture availability during the early to middle Holocene was associated with stronger monsoonal influence and potentially additional moisture supplied by the westerlies. Subsequent drying coincided with weakening monsoonal influence and changes in the position of the westerly jet that may have reduced effective moisture transport to the study region. These findings highlight the importance of both circulation intensity and spatial changes in atmospheric circulation and associated moisture transport pathways in shaping long-term hydroclimatic evolution across the westerly-monsoon transition zone.

item.title: Extreme-Amplitude MJO Events: Multi-scale Origins and Amplified Role in Compound Extremes
item.dc:creator: Guosen Chen
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: predictability, climate extreme
The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), the dominant mode of tropical intraseasonal climate variability, significantly influences global weather. It often departs from a regular cycle, exhibiting erratic behavior that occasionally amplifies into exceptionally high-amplitude events, whose characteristics and global impacts remain poorly constrained. Here, we show that boreal winter extreme-amplitude MJO (EA-MJO) events, whose amplitude measured by convection-based MJO indices exceeds the 90th percentile of the historical distribution, arise from enhanced energy transfer to planetary scales, leading to a zonal spatial expansion of MJO. Integrated observational analysis and theoretical modeling reveal that this expansion is facilitated by combined effects of favorable background states and high-frequency transients. Specifically, a concurrent eastward extension of the Indo-Pacific warm pool provides a sustained high-moisture corridor that supports organized convection and promotes MJO intensification by consuming background moisture. Meanwhile, a suppression of westward-propagating high-frequency equatorial Rossby waves from central-to-western Pacific reduces destructive interference, enabling farther eastward MJO propagation and triggering the onset of EA-MJO events. Compared to moderate MJO events, EA-MJOs substantially increase the occurrence of concurrent climate extremes, triggering more frequent compound wet-cold extremes and hot-dry extremes across different regions of China. The revealed multi-scale interaction governing EA-MJO genesis, fueled by low-frequency oceanic states and triggered by high-frequency wave variability, charts a tangible course toward their subseasonal-to-seasonal predictability, with direct implications for early warning of high-impact compound extremes.

item.title: Resolved gravity wave momentum flux dataset based on the ERA5 reanalysis
item.dc:creator: Zuzana Procházková, Petr Šácha
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: reanalysis
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Energy and momentum are redistributed in the atmosphere by gravity waves. Here, we present a dataset of zonal-mean gravity wave momentum fluxes, a quantity that describes momentum transport. Derived from a reanalysis, the dataset provides information on these waves for 44 years period, with unusually high temporal, vertical and meridional resolution. The data are compared with satellite observation and we illustrate potential use in studying climate effects of gravity waves in the atmosphere.

item.title: Mobility-driven changes in urban air quality during the COVID-19 lockdown: Evidence from the Baridhara monitoring station, Dhaka, Bangladesh
item.dc:creator: Maheen Zaman, Md. Jobayer Khan, Md. Ahnaf Zaman
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: proxy, ensemble, machine learning
by Maheen Zaman, Md. Jobayer Khan, Md. Ahnaf Zaman The COVID-19 lockdown created a natural experiment for examining how large changes in human activity coincided with urban air-quality change. This study evaluated daily Air Quality Index (AQI) and PM2.5 measured at the U.S. Embassy Baridhara monitoring station in northern Dhaka, Bangladesh, using a 2016–2022 air-quality record, Bangladesh-level Google Community Mobility Reports, and NASA POWER meteorological variables. Because the mobility series were available only at national scale, they were treated as contextual proxies for broad activity change rather than as direct measurements of mobility within Dhaka. Four complementary approaches were applied: a SARIMAX interrupted time-series model, partial wavelet coherence, artificial-neural-network weather normalization selected from eight machine-learning models by five-fold time-series cross-validation, and eight mobility-prediction models interpreted with SHAP. The interrupted time series identified a large immediate decline at lockdown onset (AQI −90.3 units; PM2.5 −110.0 µg m − 3; p < 0.001; adjusted R2 = 0.80 and 0.87). After meteorological adjustment, mobility–pollution coherence remained moderate, with the strongest bands at 8–16 days for AQI and 2–4 days for PM2.5. A direct correlation analysis, performed to complement the normalization, showed that the meteorology–pollution relationships of the lockdown months were indistinguishable in sign and magnitude from those of the pre-pandemic and post-lockdown March–June windows. Random Forest best predicted weather-normalized AQI (R2 = 0.60), while XGBoost best predicted weather-normalized PM2.5 (R2 = 0.66); confidence intervals overlapped among leading ensembles. SHAP indicated that residential, grocery and pharmacy, workplace, and transit mobility were the most influential predictors in the fitted models. The findings show a temporary, weather-independent association between broad mobility change and air quality at one monitoring site, but they do not establish a city-wide or causal effect. The results support transport-demand and emissions-management strategies that can deliver local air-quality benefits while complementing climate-mitigation goals.

item.title: Glacier thickness, thermal regime and subjective uncertainty from ground-penetrating radar of 25 Svalbard glaciers
item.dc:creator: Erik Schytt Mannerfelt, Ursula Enzenhofer, Satu Innanen, Jogscha Miriam Abderhalden, Karlijn Ploeg, Johannes Brunner, … (+6)
item.description:
Journal of Glaciology — matched: glacier
Glacier thickness and thermal regime control glacier dynamics and long-term evolution, but observations are sparse at regional scales. These variables can be measured using ground-penetrating radar (GPR), which requires manual or automated interpretation. Interpretation often depends on more than radar signal waveform analysis, yet the resulting subjectivity has not previously been thoroughly quantified. We present 699 km of ground-based GPR data from 25 glaciers in Svalbard, after crowd-sourcing glacier bed and cold-temperate transition surface (CTS) interpretations from 41 contributors. We find that subjective uncertainty is usually smaller than instrument-related uncertainties for the glacier bed, though notable exceptions exist from off-nadir reflections or occlusion by temperate ice. CTS interpretations have higher spreads and show qualitative disagreement in the required amount of scatter to be considered as temperate ice. Our thermal regime consensus estimates reveal a wide diversity in temperate ice extent and distribution between glaciers, as well as insights into the thermal structure of glaciers with surge-related histories. Our thickness consensus agrees with previous measurements, and we show that thickness inversion model performance varies with thermal regime. These data are made available to enable novel applications and automated bed/CTS detection methods that acknowledge interpretation uncertainty.
